title: Freelance Invoice Dispute Kit
description: For when a client pushes back on an invoice. Triage the 7 common dispute types, reply with ready-to-edit emails for each, split off the undisputed amount so it gets paid now, set your lowest acceptable number before you negotiate, and put the outcome in writing. Includes a full worked example, an evidence log, a dispute tracker and a prevention checklist.

files.01-first-48-hours.md:
# The First 48 Hours

The first reply sets the tone for the whole dispute. Clients who feel heard tend to pay. Clients who feel attacked dig in.

## Within a few hours: acknowledge

Send a short holding reply. Don't argue, don't concede, don't explain yet.

> Hi [name],
>
> Thanks for letting me know. I want to make sure I understand your concerns properly, so I'm going to go back through the project notes and approvals and come back to you with a full reply by [day, date].
>
> In the meantime, could you tell me which parts of the invoice you're comfortable with, and which parts you'd like to discuss? That will help me focus on the right things.
>
> Thanks,
> [your name]

That last question matters. It nudges the client to separate the undisputed amount without you demanding it yet.

## Day 1: do this

- [ ] Re-read their email twice. Underline every specific complaint, so you answer each one.
- [ ] Find the proposal, quote, contract or scope of work they agreed to.
- [ ] Find every written approval ("looks great", "approved", "go ahead", signed-off stages).
- [ ] Find every change request and whether you priced or confirmed it.
- [ ] Note delivery dates and how the work was delivered (file share, email, live site).
- [ ] Record all of it in `evidence-log.csv`.
- [ ] Decide the dispute type using `02-dispute-triage.md`.

## Day 1: don't do this

- Don't reply while annoyed. Draft, wait an hour, then edit.
- Don't threaten (late fees, collections, reviews) in the first reply. Save escalation for when it's clearly needed.
- Don't offer a discount in the holding reply. You don't yet know if one is warranted.
- Don't start "fixing" work before the fix and the invoice outcome are agreed.
- Don't cc extra people on the client side unless it's normal for this project.
- Don't post about it publicly, even anonymously. Clients find these things.

## Day 2: the full reply

Use the matching script in `03-response-scripts.md`. A good full reply has five parts:

1. **Thanks + empathy** (one line): "I understand this isn't what you expected to see."
2. **What was agreed:** quote the scope or approval, briefly, with attachments.
3. **Your honest read:** where they're right, say so. Where they're not, show the record.
4. **The split:** "The [items] aren't in question, so I've reissued those as invoice [number] for [amount], due [date]."
5. **A way forward with a date:** one or two options, and when you need an answer.

## Questions that often unlock a dispute

- "Is this about the work itself, or the total?"
- "Who on your side needs to be happy with this before it can be paid?"
- "What would 'done' look like to you?"
- "Is there a budget or approval issue on your end I can help with, such as splitting it across two months or adding a PO number?"
- "If we fixed [specific thing], would the rest of the invoice be fine to pay?"
files.02-dispute-triage.md:
# Dispute Triage: Which Kind Is It?

Read the client's message and pick the closest type. If it's a mix, deal with the admin issues first (they're the easiest to clear), then the substantive ones.

## Quick picker

| What they say | Likely type | Jump to |
|---|---|---|
| "The amount is wrong" / "We were quoted less" | 1. Amount or admin error | Type 1 |
| "This isn't finished" / "It doesn't work" | 2. Quality or completion | Type 2 |
| "We never asked for this" | 3. Scope disagreement | Type 3 |
| "Nobody approved these extra hours" | 4. Unapproved overage | Type 4 |
| "Can you do it for less?" after delivery | 5. Post-delivery discount ask | Type 5 |
| "Our finance team rejected it" | 6. Process or paperwork | Type 6 |
| Silence after you flagged the overdue invoice | 7. Avoidance | Type 7 |

---

## Type 1: Amount or admin error

**What it really is:** A number doesn't match what they expect: wrong rate, a duplicate line, tax treatment, a missing deposit credit.

**Ask yourself:** Is my invoice actually wrong? Check the quote, the deposit, and every line.

**Best move:** If you made a mistake, own it fast and reissue a corrected invoice the same day. If you didn't, walk them through the maths line by line, with the original quote attached.

**Undisputed amount:** Usually everything except the lines in question.

---

## Type 2: Quality or completion

**What it really is:** They believe the work isn't to the standard or isn't done.

**Ask yourself:** Does the work meet the written brief? Is there a real defect (a bug, a typo, a missing deliverable), or is it a matter of taste after approval?

**Best move:**
- *Real defect:* fix it promptly, at no charge, and agree in writing that the invoice will be paid once it's fixed.
- *Taste after approval:* point to the approval kindly, then offer further changes as a new, priced change request.
- *Ambiguous brief:* consider a middle path, such as one extra round of revisions, then final payment.

**Undisputed amount:** Stages or deliverables that are complete and approved.

---

## Type 3: Scope disagreement

**What it really is:** You both believe the scope said different things.

**Ask yourself:** What does the written scope literally say? Was the item mentioned in an email, a call, or not at all?

**Best move:** Quote the scope. If it's genuinely unclear, offer to split the difference on *that item only*. Add clearer wording to your next proposal.

**Undisputed amount:** Everything clearly inside the original scope.

---

## Type 4: Unapproved overage

**What it really is:** You billed more hours or more items than estimated, and they weren't told in advance.

**Ask yourself:** Did I warn them before going over? Did they agree, even informally ("keep going")?

**Best move:**
- *You warned them and they agreed:* show the message.
- *You didn't warn them:* this is the type where a concession is often fair. Consider billing the overage at a reduced rate or capping it, and fix your process (see `06-prevention-checklist.md`).

**Undisputed amount:** Everything up to the original estimate.

---

## Type 5: Post-delivery discount ask

**What it really is:** Budget pressure, buyer's remorse, or testing whether you'll fold. There's no specific complaint about the work.

**Ask yourself:** Is there any real issue I'm missing? Do I want more work from this client?

**Best move:** Politely hold your price. If you want to offer something, offer *value* rather than a cut: a payment plan, or a small extra (a short handover call, a template) instead of money off.

**Undisputed amount:** Technically all of it. Ask for full payment by a date.

---

## Type 6: Process or paperwork

**What it really is:** Missing PO number, wrong entity name, wrong address, missing tax ID, not set up as a supplier, wrong approver.

**Ask yourself:** What exactly does their finance team need?

**Best move:** Ask for the specific requirement, fix it the same day, reissue, and ask for the new expected payment date. Note it for future invoices to this client.

**Undisputed amount:** All of it, once the paperwork is fixed.

---

## Type 7: Avoidance

**What it really is:** No formal complaint, just silence, vague delays or "I'll look into it."

**Ask yourself:** Am I emailing the right person? Has anyone actually said no?

**Best move:** Change channel (call, or message a different contact who approves payments), ask a direct yes/no question ("Is anything about the invoice holding up payment?"), and set a date. If they then raise a complaint, it becomes one of types 1 to 6.

**Undisputed amount:** All of it until they name a problem.

---

## Your triage notes

| Question | Your answer |
|---|---|
| Dispute type(s) |  |
| Exact complaint, in their words |  |
| What the written scope says |  |
| Evidence I have (see evidence log) |  |
| Where they have a fair point |  |
| Undisputed amount |  |
| Disputed amount |  |
| Do I want to keep this client? (yes / maybe / no) |  |
| My lowest acceptable outcome |  |
files.03-response-scripts.md:
# Response Scripts

Replace everything in [square brackets]. Attach the evidence you reference. Keep the tone even: firm on facts, warm on the relationship.

---

## Type 1: Amount or admin error

### 1a. You made a mistake

> Subject: Corrected invoice [number]
>
> Hi [name],
>
> You're right, and thanks for catching it. I [charged the old rate / included the deposit twice / missed the agreed discount]. I've attached a corrected invoice, [new number], for [amount], which replaces [old number].
>
> Payment terms are unchanged, so it's due on [date]. Sorry for the hassle.
>
> Thanks,
> [your name]

### 1b. The invoice is correct

> Subject: Re: Invoice [number]
>
> Hi [name],
>
> Thanks for checking this. Here's how the total breaks down against the quote from [date] (attached):
>
> - [Item 1]: [amount], as quoted
> - [Item 2]: [amount], as quoted
> - [Change request from date]: [amount], approved by [name] on [date] (email attached)
> - Less deposit paid on [date]: -[amount]
> - **Balance: [amount]**
>
> If I've misunderstood which part looks off, let me know and I'll go through it with you. Otherwise, the balance is due on [date].
>
> Thanks,
> [your name]

---

## Type 2: Quality or completion

### 2a. There's a real defect

> Hi [name],
>
> Thanks for flagging [specific problem]. You're right that it doesn't [work / match the brief], and I'll have it fixed by [date] at no extra cost.
>
> The rest of the project ([list]) is complete and was approved on [date], so I've split the invoice: [number A] for [amount] covers that and is due on [date]. [Number B] for [amount] covers [item] and will be due [X] days after I deliver the fix.
>
> Does that work for you?
>
> Thanks,
> [your name]

### 2b. A taste change after approval

> Hi [name],
>
> Thanks for the feedback, and I understand wanting it to feel right.
>
> For context, we finalised [item] on [date] when you approved [version] (attached), and the invoice reflects that approved work, so it stands as issued.
>
> I'm happy to make the changes you've described as a small follow-on piece. I estimate [hours/price] and could start on [date]. Want me to go ahead?
>
> Thanks,
> [your name]

### 2c. The brief was genuinely unclear

> Hi [name],
>
> Looking back at the brief, I can see how we read [point] differently. It says "[quote]", which I took to mean [your reading].
>
> To keep things moving, I'll do one more round of changes on [item] to bring it closer to what you had in mind, at no charge, delivered by [date]. Once that's done, the invoice is payable in full within [X] days. Anything beyond that round would be quoted separately.
>
> Shall I go ahead on that basis?
>
> Thanks,
> [your name]

---

## Type 3: Scope disagreement

> Hi [name],
>
> Thanks for raising this. I've gone back to the agreed scope from [date] (attached). It lists [quote the relevant line], and [disputed item] was added on [date] when you asked for [request] (email attached).
>
> [If unclear:] I can see the wording on [item] could be read either way, so I'm happy to meet you halfway on that one line: [reduced amount] instead of [original].
>
> The rest of the invoice covers work that's clearly in scope, so I've reissued that part as [number] for [amount], due on [date].
>
> Thanks,
> [your name]

---

## Type 4: Unapproved overage

### 4a. You did warn them

> Hi [name],
>
> On [date] I let you know we were heading past the estimate because of [reason], and you replied "[their words]" (attached). The extra [hours/items] on the invoice are that work.
>
> If it would help with budgeting, I can split the overage across [two/three] monthly payments.
>
> Thanks,
> [your name]

### 4b. You didn't warn them (be fair)

> Hi [name],
>
> You're right that I should have flagged it before going over the estimate. That's on me.
>
> The extra [hours] were for [reason], and the work is done and delivered. As a fair middle ground, I've capped the overage at [amount] instead of [original amount], and reissued the invoice as [number] for [total], due on [date].
>
> Going forward, I'll check in with you before going more than [10%] over any estimate.
>
> Thanks,
> [your name]

---

## Type 5: Post-delivery discount ask

> Hi [name],
>
> Thanks for being upfront about the budget. I'm glad the [project] came together well.
>
> I'm not able to reduce the fee, because it reflects the scope we agreed on [date]. What I can do is make it easier to manage: [split it into two payments, on date and date / extend the due date to date].
>
> Let me know which works best.
>
> Thanks,
> [your name]

*If you want to give something:* offer a non-cash extra, such as a 30-minute handover call, a style guide or a set of templates. It protects your rate for future work.

---

## Type 6: Process or paperwork

> Hi [name],
>
> Thanks for letting me know. To get this through your finance team, could you send me:
>
> - [the PO number / the correct legal entity name / billing address / your supplier form]
>
> I'll reissue the invoice the same day I receive it. Could you also let me know when the next payment run is, so I can make sure it's included?
>
> Thanks,
> [your name]

---

## Type 7: Avoidance

> Hi [name],
>
> I've sent a couple of notes about invoice [number] for [amount], due on [date], and I haven't heard back, which isn't like you. I want to check: is there anything about the invoice or the work that's holding up payment?
>
> If there is, let me know and I'll sort it out. If not, could you confirm a payment date by [date]?
>
> Thanks,
> [your name]

---

## Follow-ups

### Confirming a phone call

> Hi [name],
>
> Thanks for the call today. To confirm what we agreed:
>
> - [Item/outcome 1]
> - [Item/outcome 2]
> - Revised invoice [number] for [amount], due on [date]
>
> If I've got any of that wrong, let me know by [date]. Otherwise I'll go ahead on this basis.
>
> Thanks,
> [your name]

### When the agreed date passes

> Hi [name],
>
> On [date] we agreed that [amount] would be paid by [date]. I haven't received it yet. Could you let me know today when it will be sent?
>
> Until it's settled, I'll need to pause work on [current project / new requests].
>
> Thanks,
> [your name]

### Final written notice (only once the resolution has failed)

> Hi [name],
>
> Despite our agreement on [date], invoice [number] for [amount] remains unpaid. Please pay in full by [date, about 7 days out].
>
> If I don't receive payment or hear from you by then, I'll [take the next steps available to me under our agreement / step you have checked applies where you are].
>
> Regards,
> [your name]
files.04-settlement-options.md:
# Settlement Options and Your Floor

## Step 1: Set your floor before you talk

Work this out privately before any call or reply where money is discussed. It stops you agreeing to something on the spot that you'll regret.

| Line | Your number |
|---|---|
| A. Invoice total |  |
| B. Undisputed amount (should be paid regardless) |  |
| C. Disputed amount (A - B) |  |
| D. How strong is your evidence on C? (strong / mixed / weak) |  |
| E. Hours a long dispute would cost you (chasing, calls, rework) |  |
| F. Your hourly rate |  |
| G. Cost of a long dispute (E x F) |  |
| H. Future work this client is likely worth over the next year |  |
| **Floor** = B + the share of C you won't go below |  |

**Rules of thumb (not rules):**

- *Strong evidence:* floor is usually B + 90-100% of C.
- *Mixed evidence:* B + 50-80% of C.
- *Weak evidence (you didn't flag the overage, the brief was vague):* B + 0-50% of C.
- If G is bigger than the disputed amount, a quick settlement may be worth more than "winning".
- If H is large, being generous on a small disputed amount can be a good investment. If H is zero, you can afford to be firmer.

Decide your floor, write it down, and don't move below it in the moment. If the client offers less, say "Let me think about that and come back to you tomorrow."

## Step 2: Pick a resolution

### 1. Correct and reissue
**Use when:** the invoice had a genuine error (Type 1).
**How:** cancel the old invoice, issue a new one with a new number and a note "replaces [old number]". Keep the original due date if the error was small.

### 2. Split the invoice
**Use when:** part of the invoice is undisputed (most disputes).
**How:** reissue as two invoices: the undisputed part due now, the disputed part on hold until resolved. This is often the fastest way to get most of your money.

### 3. Fix, then pay
**Use when:** there's a real defect (Type 2a).
**How:** agree in writing exactly what will be fixed, by when, and that payment is due [X] days after the fix is delivered. Don't accept "and then we'll see".

### 4. Partial credit
**Use when:** you share some responsibility (unflagged overage, ambiguous brief).
**How:** issue a credit note (or a reissued invoice) for the agreed reduction, and state it is "in full and final settlement of [invoice]" so the matter is closed. Keep the reduction tied to a specific line, not a general percentage off everything.

### 5. Payment plan
**Use when:** the client accepts the debt but can't pay it all at once.
**How:** list each instalment amount and date in writing. Say what happens if an instalment is missed (for example, the full remaining balance becomes due). Send a reminder two days before each date.

### 6. Value instead of money off
**Use when:** a discount ask has no real basis (Type 5) but you want goodwill.
**How:** add a small, low-cost extra (handover call, templates, a short training video) and keep the invoice amount unchanged.

## Step 3: Put it in writing

Whatever you agree, confirm it in one email with:

- [ ] The invoice number(s) and amounts
- [ ] What each side will do, and by when
- [ ] The final amount and due date(s)
- [ ] That this settles the dispute on that invoice
- [ ] What happens if a date is missed

Log the outcome in `dispute-tracker.csv`.
files.05-worked-example.md:
# Worked Example: A Website Invoice Disputed on Three Fronts

*A fictional example to show the process end to end.*

## The setup

Alex is a freelance web designer. Client: a small accountancy practice, contact Morgan.

- Agreed fixed fee: **$4,800** for a homepage and four inner pages
- Deposit (25%) paid at the start: **$1,200**
- Mid-project, Morgan emailed: "Can we add a blog page template too?" Alex replied with a price of $600, and Morgan wrote back "Yes, go ahead."
- Near the end, Alex spent 6 extra hours loading the client's content into the pages. This wasn't in the scope, and Alex didn't mention it before doing it. Alex's rate: $100/hour.

**Final invoice INV-052:**

| Line | Amount |
|---|---|
| Remaining project fee ($4,800 - $1,200 deposit) | $3,600 |
| Blog page template (change request, approved by email) | $600 |
| Content loading, 6 hours at $100 | $600 |
| **Total due** | **$4,800** |

Terms: 14 days.

## The pushback (day 0)

Morgan replies: "We're surprised by this. We thought the blog was part of the site, we never asked for 6 extra hours, and the contact form on the site still doesn't work. We'd like to discuss before paying."

## Alex's holding reply (same day)

> Hi Morgan, thanks for letting me know. I'm going to go back through the project notes and come back to you with a full reply by Thursday. In the meantime, could you tell me if there's anything on the invoice you're comfortable with? That'll help me focus.

## Triage (day 1)

| Complaint | Type | Evidence | Fair point? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Blog template "part of the site" | 3. Scope | Scope lists 5 pages; email of 12 Sept approves blog at $600 | No: written approval |
| 6 extra hours | 4. Unapproved overage | No warning sent | **Yes**: Alex didn't flag it |
| Contact form broken | 2. Quality (real defect) | Alex tests it: confirmed broken after a plugin update | **Yes** |

Evidence log rows added: scope document, 12 Sept approval email, launch email, form test screenshot.

## Setting the floor

| Line | Amount |
|---|---|
| A. Invoice total | $4,800 |
| B. Undisputed (remaining project fee, once the form is fixed) | $3,600 |
| C. Disputed (blog + hours) | $1,200 |
| Blog: strong evidence, keep 100% | $600 |
| Hours: weak (not flagged), willing to go to 0% | $0 |
| **Floor** | **$4,200** |

Alex also notes: Morgan's practice is likely to want ongoing updates (roughly $1,500 a year). Worth keeping the relationship.

## Alex's full reply (day 2)

> Hi Morgan,
>
> Thanks for your patience. I've gone through everything, and here's where I've landed:
>
> **Contact form:** You're right, it broke after a plugin update. I've fixed it today and tested it. Please send a test message and let me know it arrives.
>
> **Blog template:** This was added on 12 September. I quoted $600 and you replied "Yes, go ahead" (attached), so that line stands.
>
> **Content loading:** You're right that I should have checked with you before doing the extra 6 hours. That's on me. I've reduced that line from $600 to $300.
>
> I've reissued the invoice as INV-052A for $4,500, replacing INV-052, due 14 days from today. Going forward, I'll always check with you before doing anything outside the agreed scope.
>
> Thanks,
> Alex

## Outcome

- Morgan tests the form, confirms it works, and accepts the revised invoice.
- Paid in full on day 11: **$4,500** (Alex's floor was $4,200).
- Alex conceded $300 on the one point where Morgan was right, kept the $600 that was clearly approved, and kept the client. Two months later, Morgan books a $750 update.

## What Alex changed afterwards

- Adds a line to every proposal: "Work outside this scope will be quoted and approved in writing before it starts."
- Sets a personal rule: message the client before going 10% past any estimate.
- Adds a 30-day "fix it free" period for defects to the proposal, so a broken form becomes a support task, not a payment dispute.

## The tracker row

```
dispute_id,client,invoice,invoice_total,undisputed,disputed,type,opened,holding_reply_sent,full_reply_due,floor,offer_made,agreed_amount,status,next_step,next_step_date,paid_date,lesson

```
files.06-prevention-checklist.md:
# Prevention Checklist

Most invoice disputes are decided long before the invoice is sent. Run through this list for your next project.

## In the proposal or contract

- [ ] Deliverables listed one by one, with quantities ("5 pages", "2 rounds of revisions", "up to 1,500 words")
- [ ] A short "not included" list for the things clients often assume (content entry, stock images, hosting, extra rounds)
- [ ] How changes are handled: "Work outside this scope is quoted and approved in writing before it starts."
- [ ] What counts as approval (a written "approved" on each stage, or no feedback within [X] working days)
- [ ] Payment terms, deposit and stage payments, and what happens if a payment is late
- [ ] Who approves invoices on the client side, and what they need (PO number, entity name, supplier setup)
- [ ] A defect-fix window ("bugs reported within 30 days of launch are fixed at no charge")

## During the project

- [ ] Get written sign-off at each stage, not just at the end
- [ ] Confirm every change request in writing, with a price, before starting it
- [ ] Message the client before going more than 10% past any estimate
- [ ] Send a short weekly or milestone update so nothing on the invoice is a surprise
- [ ] Save approvals and change requests into a project folder as they happen (or add them to `evidence-log.csv`)

## When invoicing

- [ ] Each line maps to something in the scope or an approved change request
- [ ] Reference approvals on the invoice ("Blog template: change request approved 12 Sept")
- [ ] Deposit and any credits shown clearly
- [ ] PO number, correct legal entity and billing details included
- [ ] Sent to the person who pays, with the person who approves in copy if needed
- [ ] A friendly heads-up 3 days before the due date

## After a dispute

- [ ] Write one sentence in the "lesson" column of `dispute-tracker.csv`
- [ ] Update your proposal template with the fix
- [ ] Decide whether to change terms for this client (larger deposit, stage payments, shorter terms)
files.README.md:
# Freelance Invoice Dispute Kit

A client has pushed back on an invoice. Maybe they say the work isn't finished, the number is higher than they expected, something was "never approved", or they want a discount now that the work is delivered. This kit helps you answer calmly, separate the money that is actually in dispute from the money that isn't, and get paid without wrecking the relationship (or giving away more than you need to).

## What's inside

| File | What it's for |
|---|---|
| `README.md` | This guide and the 5-step process |
| `01-first-48-hours.md` | What to do (and not do) right after the pushback lands |
| `02-dispute-triage.md` | Work out which of 7 dispute types you're facing and what each one really needs |
| `03-response-scripts.md` | Ready-to-edit emails for every dispute type, plus follow-ups |
| `04-settlement-options.md` | Six ways to resolve it, and how to set your "lowest acceptable" number before you negotiate |
| `05-worked-example.md` | A full dispute from first email to payment, with the numbers |
| `06-prevention-checklist.md` | Changes to your process so the next invoice doesn't get disputed |
| `evidence-log.csv` | One row per piece of evidence: approvals, emails, change requests, delivery receipts |
| `dispute-tracker.csv` | Track every open dispute, what's undisputed, what you offered and what's next |

## The 5-step process

1. **Pause, don't fire back.** Acknowledge the email the same day in one or two lines. Promise a full reply by a specific date (usually within 2 working days). See `01-first-48-hours.md`.
2. **Name the dispute.** Use `02-dispute-triage.md` to decide which type it is. Most disputes are one of seven kinds, and each needs a different reply. A quality complaint handled like a discount request goes badly.
3. **Gather the record.** Fill in `evidence-log.csv`: the proposal or contract, the approvals, the change requests, delivery dates. Write down what you can show, not what you remember.
4. **Split the invoice.** Almost every dispute is about *part* of the invoice. Work out the undisputed amount and ask for that to be paid now, while you resolve the rest. This single move gets most freelancers paid faster.
5. **Offer a resolution with a deadline.** Pick from `04-settlement-options.md`, set your floor before you talk, and put the agreed outcome in writing. Log it in `dispute-tracker.csv`.

## Ground rules that keep disputes small

- Stay factual. "On 3 October you approved the homepage in writing (attached)" beats "You already said it was fine."
- Ask questions before defending. Half of disputes turn out to be a missing purchase order, a confused finance team or one unhappy stakeholder.
- Never re-do work for free *before* you've agreed what "done" means and what happens to the invoice afterwards.
- Keep everything in writing. If you talk on the phone, send a short "to confirm what we agreed" email the same day.
- Decide early whether this client is worth keeping. That changes how much you'll concede, and it's fine to answer "no".

## A note on scope

This kit is general information to help you communicate and organise. It isn't legal advice. Whether you can charge late fees or interest, what counts as acceptance, and what formal options you have (demand letters, collections, small claims) depend on your contract and where you and your client are based. If a large sum is at stake, a short consultation with a local professional is often worth it.
